items.title: Russia detains federal youth agency official and Synergy private university vice-rector over allegedly unusable online courses
items.summary:
Update : Denis Ashirov, deputy head of Russia’s youth affairs agency Rosmolodezh, has been detained in a fraud investigation involving contracts with Synergy University, sources told RBC. 
 Authorities searched Synergy University as part of a theft investigation and detained Vice Rector Mikhail Yerofeyev, REN TV and TASS reported.

Kommersant reported that Yerofeyev is suspected of stealing funds while carrying out a government contract and is being held in a temporary detention facility. The investigation concerns a contract worth 31.5 million rubles that Synergy received in 2023, the newspaper reported.

Investigators allege that subcontractors did most of the work to create an online professional development course, spending no more than 13.5 million rubles. However, the university received full payment after the work was accepted, and investigators believe its management may have stolen or embezzled the remaining 18 million rubles. The resulting courses also proved unusable in practice, Kommersant reported.

The university said the searches and other investigative actions concern two government contracts signed with Rosmolodezh in 2023 and 2024. Synergy maintains that it completed the work on time and that the educational programs it created “actually worked”: More than 50,000 people completed the training, and more than 36,000 received professional development certificates, the university said in a statement.

The university also said it was operating as usual and cooperating with investigators. It said investigators had opened a case over an alleged crime without…
items.t: Russia detains federal youth agency official and Synergy private university vice-rector over allegedly unusable online courses

items.title: Russian MMA fighter Usman Nurmagomedov gets six months in a UAE prison over hotel brawl with former UFC champion Merab Dvalishvili
items.summary:
Russian mixed martial arts fighter Usman Nurmagomedov has been sentenced to six months in jail in the United Arab Emirates over a fight with Georgian fighter Merab Dvalishvili , a source told TASS.

Several other members of Nurmagomedov’s team also received six-month sentences and large fines.

The Abu Dhabi Judicial Department said a court had convicted 10 people in connection with the fight but did not release their names. Each received a six-month prison sentence and a fine of 300,000 dirhams (about 6.7 million rubles), with deportation to follow their prison term.

A mass brawl involving Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili, a UFC champion from Georgia, broke out in a hotel lobby in Abu Dhabi on November 11. Nurmagomedov approached Dvalishvili while he was giving an interview and slapped him. MMA outlets reported that Nurmagomedov was retaliating because Dvalishvili had earlier slapped a friend of Usman’s brother, Umar Nurmagomedov. A video posted later shows Nurmagomedov approaching Dvalishvili from behind.

The National reported that Dvalishvili and his friend were each fined 50,000 dirhams for “disturbing public security and assaulting others” but received no jail time.

items.title: Russia moves to monitor peer-to-peer bank transfers for undeclared income
items.summary:
Russia’s Finance Ministry has proposed requiring the Central Bank to give the Federal Tax Service information about individuals “whose account transactions show signs that they regularly receive income from other individuals.”

The ministry proposed the amendment ahead of the second reading of a bill in the budget package, Interfax reported. The relevant State Duma committee plans to consider it on November 15.

Under the proposal, the Bank of Russia would analyze transactions in individuals’ accounts and pass information to the Federal Tax Service if it found signs of “receiving income from other individuals.” The tax service could then request statements for those accounts from banks.

The criteria for identifying signs of “regularly receiving income from other individuals” would be set separately, along with the format and frequency of the Central Bank’s reports to tax authorities.

Tax inspectors can currently request bank statements for individuals who are not registered as sole proprietors only if authorities have issued a decision to collect a tax debt or a tax audit authorized by a higher tax authority is underway. The Finance Ministry’s proposed amendment would add a new basis for such requests: information from the Central Bank.

In March, Vedomosti reported that the Finance Ministry was drafting amendments to tighten scrutiny of transfers between individuals. Under the ministry’s plan as reported at the time, the Federal Tax Service would obtain information from banks about individuals’ account openings and closures, their bank cards, and their income…
items.t: Russia moves to monitor peer-to-peer bank transfers for undeclared income

items.title: Russia demands Finland leave NATO, Bild reports. Moscow denies it, and Helsinki is outraged.
items.summary:
The German tabloid Bild reported on November 13 that Russia had demanded Finland’s withdrawal from NATO as part of peace talks on Ukraine. The outlet said Russian representatives put forward the demand at unspecified informal talks on ending the war.

Russia officially denied the report. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters: “I’m not aware of this. No, [such a proposal] was not put forward. It certainly wasn’t discussed.”

Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen called Russia’s demand for a reduced NATO presence in countries bordering Russia a test of U.S. and European resolve during the negotiations.

“Russia wants European NATO countries to set limits on their own operations to serve Russian interests, and such things are not negotiable,” Häkkänen said. “Even suggesting such things is simply outrageous. Russia knows that,” he added.

According to unconfirmed information reported by Bild, Moscow proposed that Russia receive all of Donbas and retain the Ukrainian territories it occupies; that NATO agree not to establish military bases in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania; and that Ukraine adopt nonaligned status, abandon its plans to join NATO, and refrain from using the ports of Odesa and Mykolaiv as naval bases.

Russia is also seeking freedom of navigation in the Black and Baltic seas and demanding that Moldova become a federal republic. If Moldova joins the EU, Moscow wants it to allow independence referendums in Transnistria and Gagauzia.

In exchange, Russia is offering to withdraw nuclear weapons from Belarus, refrain from deploying intermediate-range…
items.t: Russia demands Finland leave NATO, Bild reports. Moscow denies it, and Helsinki is outraged.

items.title: Russia adopts state standard for ‘traditional Russian cuisine,’ including ‘Little Russian’ borscht, Chicken Kiev, and okroshka made with kvass, not kefir
items.summary:
Rosstandart, Russia’s federal standards agency, has approved a state standard (GOST) titled “Traditional Russian cuisine: Recommendations for preparing dishes” (registered users can view it  here ). The document includes recipes, preparation methods, and serving suggestions for 132 dishes.

An Industry and Trade Ministry working group developed the standard. Its members included officials and representatives from the restaurant industry. Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov said the document was “not an attempt to regulate everything, but a guide that guarantees consumers authenticity and high quality.”

“[Today] only 1% of restaurants in the country describe themselves as serving Russian cuisine. In effect, we’ve lost an important part of our cultural identity,” the minister said. He said the standard should “reverse this trend.”

Roskachestvo, Russia’s quality watchdog, said the standard aims to “catalog Russian dishes, their historical roots, and the principles for using authentic ingredients.” Compliance is voluntary, said Igor Bukharov, president of the Federation of Restaurateurs and Hoteliers and a member of the working group.

The standard provides guidelines for making blini, vinegret salad, stuffed cabbage rolls, porridge, kolobok buns, Russian-style crayfish, and more than 100 other dishes.

For example, the authors recommend making okroshka with bread kvass that has a “pronounced sour taste.” Cucumber or berry brine may be added, but using kefir or other fermented dairy products in okroshka is “not recommended.”

The document lists several versions of…
items.t: Russia adopts state standard for ‘traditional Russian cuisine,’ including ‘Little Russian’ borscht, Chicken Kiev, and okroshka made with kvass, not kefir

items.title: German intelligence agencies gain powers to hack foreign IT systems and recruit informants as young as 16
items.summary:
Germany’s parliament has approved a bill significantly expanding the powers of the country’s intelligence agencies. The law aims to counter espionage, terrorism, and sabotage, the newspaper Die Welt reported.

The changes apply to the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (BND).

The law allows the agencies to:

Secretly enter homes Carry out cyberattacks on foreign IT systems Delete or alter data or redirect internet traffic Use AI to analyze biometric data Recruit teenagers 16 and older as informants in exceptional cases 
 A special body, including former judges, will review whether proposed measures are legal before the agencies carry them out.

The authorities said the law was needed because of growing hybrid threats from Russia, China, and Iran.

items.title: After detaining ‘Polish spies’ in Kaliningrad, the FSB released their alleged messages in Polish. Native speakers say they contain errors and unnatural phrasing.
items.summary:
Polish-language messages released by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) alongside its announcement that Polish citizens had been detained in the Kaliningrad region have raised doubts among native speakers, the news outlet Agentstvo reported.

On November 11, the FSB said a Polish intelligence “spy network” had been operating in the Kaliningrad region and that two “agents” had been detained on espionage charges.

Russian authorities allege that the detainees collected and passed on information about Russian military personnel and Defense Ministry facilities. Two statements ( 1 , 2) from the regional court confirm that both detainees are Polish citizens. One was arrested back on July 30, while the other was detained on October 28.

The FSB also released a video of the detainees that showed part of a WhatsApp exchange between a “Polish intelligence agent and his handler.” According to the FSB’s translation, the “agent” and “handler” were discussing the appearance, age, and rank of an officer working at the border.

On Polish-language X, the person behind the account KrzysiekWSK drew attention to screenshots from the FSB video. Agentstvo also asked two native Polish speakers to examine the exchange. They identified the following problems:

Both participants make mistakes. The odd expression “robić rozmowy” (translated by the FSB as “communicates”) is not used in Poland. “Na granice” (translated by the FSB as “at the border”) appears instead of “na granicy.” “Napiewnie” (translated by the FSB as “probably”) appears instead of “na pewno,” as does “na powrocie” instead of…
items.t: After detaining ‘Polish spies’ in Kaliningrad, the FSB released their alleged messages in Polish. Native speakers say they contain errors and unnatural phrasing.

items.title: German counterintelligence confirms it is questioning Russians at Berlin airport, citing a ‘high threat level’
items.summary:
Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the country’s domestic intelligence agency, confirmed to  iStories and Deutsche Welle that it is questioning Russians at Berlin’s airport.

The agency said the threats facing Germany are “documented in considerable detail and remain highly fluid,” so it is “constantly adapting its measures to the persistently high threat level.” It said it conducts various measures, which “include questioning people,” within its legal authority.

IStories also asked Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) about reports that someone had tried to recruit one of the Russian women stopped for questioning at Berlin’s airport and that she was later barred from entering the Schengen Area.

The BND declined to comment, saying it reports “on the relevant matters” to the government and the Bundestag bodies responsible for overseeing it.

In early November, Kholod reported that Russian citizens had been invited to “voluntary” interviews at Berlin’s airport since September. They were asked about the situation in Russia, mobilization, and rising prices. Airport staff approached Russians after passport control and took them to separate rooms for questioning. But the Russians were told these “interviews” were voluntary only during the questioning or afterward.

Andrei Pivovarov, a politician and former political prisoner, said that after one such interview at Berlin’s airport, a Russian woman who had arrived on a tourist visa was asked to sign an agreement to cooperate with German intelligence. She refused and was later barred from…

items.title: Godson of Russian upper house speaker Valentina Matviyenko jailed for seven days over Instagram link
items.summary:
St. Petersburg’s Smolninsky District Court sentenced Vladislav Tyulpanov, the son of Senator Vadim Tyulpanov, who died in 2017, to seven days in jail for displaying banned symbols, the city courts’ press service said. The court found him guilty under Part 1 of Article 20.3 of Russia’s Code of Administrative Offenses.

The citation stemmed from a link to Tyulpanov’s Instagram account on his Telegram channel, the courts’ press service told the news outlet Rotonda. Tyulpanov fully admitted guilt and removed the link from his profile description.

Tyulpanov is 21. He calls himself “Russia’s youngest and best-known politician.” On his website and social media accounts, he regularly emphasizes that his godmother is Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko.

Tyulpanov has tried several times to join United Russia. In 2025, he  received a membership card from the party’s Chechen branch, saying he had been “prevented” from joining in St. Petersburg. The Chechen branch soon expelled him for “discrediting” the party. He tried again to join United Russia in St. Petersburg, but his application was rejected.

St. Petersburg publications have reported ( 1 , 2 ) on Tyulpanov’s relationship with singer and porn actress Katya Sambuka, as well as his videos of himself riding in expensive cars and living in a country house.

For example, during his brief time as a United Russia member, Tyulpanov posted a video of himself riding through St. Petersburg, purportedly escorted by a traffic police car with flashing lights. He also put up flyers around the city with a link to his Instagram…
items.t: Godson of Russian upper house speaker Valentina Matviyenko jailed for seven days over Instagram link

items.title: Europe taps national security advisers to represent the continent in Russia-Ukraine peace talks
items.summary:
National security advisers from the European Union, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, and Poland will represent Europe in upcoming talks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, Bloomberg reported .

European leaders made the decision after a summit in Dublin on November 12 and 13.

European Council President António Costa and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed the makeup of the European delegation.

“Our principles and our positions in these negotiations remain well known.

“And our European team will continue to act in full unity and in close coordination with all member states,” Costa wrote on X.

A senior European official told Bloomberg that the advisers would take part in the upcoming talks at the technical level. Europe has yet to appoint representatives for negotiations at the highest level.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had previously urged European leaders to appoint representatives to take part in U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.

After talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said the three-way peace talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine would be expanded to include Europe. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had no objection to European participation. Russia’s Foreign Ministry, however, said the subject had not come up at all during Putin’s meeting with the Americans. Peskov said “a concrete decision on broadening the talks” could be made once the Kremlin “understands [the Europeans’] true intentions and willingness to help advance the peace process.”

Peace talks…
items.t: Europe taps national security advisers to represent the continent in Russia-Ukraine peace talks

items.title: Tretyakov Gallery cancels screening of film about teenagers in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod
items.summary:
The Tretyakov Gallery has canceled a screening of the documentary “My ne znakomimsya” (“We Don’t Meet New People”), about teenagers from alternative subcultures who gather in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod neighborhood. Film critic Kirill Artamonov, who curates the gallery’s “Horizons of Everyday Life” film program, said the screening had been canceled.

The screening was scheduled for November 14. Artamonov said it was being postponed “indefinitely.”

The Telegram channel Kino v Tretyakovke, which covers the gallery’s film programming, reported that the screening had been postponed because of “increased strain on technical and facilities services” caused by a sellout crowd at the ‘Léon Bakst’ exhibition.

Directed by Yulia Guskova, “My ne znakomimsya” premiered at the Beat Film Festival in June 2026. The film follows 17-year-old Gleb, who “arrives in Kitay-Gorod and immediately joins a crowd of fellow ‘alternative kids’ with dyed hair, brand-name clothes, and tattoos.” “Together, they seek and find friends, fun, and a chance to discuss pressing concerns: dating and plans for adulthood,” the film’s description says .

On the evening of November 7, mass detentions took place near the Kitay-Gorod subway station, where young people from alternative subcultures have been gathering for a second consecutive year. Estimates of the number of people detained near Gorka Park, where the teenagers usually meet, range from 150 to 200.

items.title: Three days of Ukraine peace talks and diplomatic meetings, from Abu Dhabi to Moscow to Dublin. Who met with whom — and what did they actually agree on?
items.summary:
Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, Vladimir Medinsky, and Kirill Dmitriev at talks in Moscow. November 12, 2026 
 Tuesday, November 10 . Russia, Ukraine, and the United States met in Abu Dhabi to discuss ending the war for the first time since February. The talks covered security guarantees (including for Russia) and the postwar future “amid a crisis of trust,” as well as a prisoner exchange. The talks lasted more than four hours.

Wednesday, November 11 . The second day of trilateral talks focused entirely on the postwar security architecture in Europe. Unofficially, officials in Kyiv said Russia had refused to discuss a ceasefire, territories, and energy altogether. The only agreement announced publicly was the “largest prisoner exchange of the war.” Negotiators afterward spoke of “good momentum” but acknowledged that the process is difficult. The talks ended in less than two hours.

Thursday, November 12 . Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to meet with Vladimir Putin to discuss bringing Europe into the negotiation process and ask Moscow to formulate its vision of the postwar order. Putin, in turn, proposed a joint humanitarian operation in Kostiantynivka. That evening, Kushner and Witkoff met with Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin. The outcome: all sides agreed to hold another round of talks soon , and Moscow signaled it has no objection to the participation of Europe, which now needs to  decide on its own representative.

items.title: Russia’s healthcare and education sectors have lost out on more than a trillion rubles in funding since start of full-scale war, investigation finds
items.summary:
Russia’s healthcare and education sectors have received at least one trillion rubles less than expected from the state budget since the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine, the independent Russian news outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe calculated.

The gap stems from funding for the two main components of Russia’s social sphere falling below the inflation rate. According to the outlet’s calculations, the government spent 728 billion rubles less on healthcare over the course of the war than it would have if spending had kept pace with inflation. The shortfall in education funding amounted to 322 billion rubles.

Novaya Gazeta Europe’s reporters have identified more than 800 cases of staff cuts and institution closures in the social sphere since 2021. More than a quarter of them occurred in 2026 — a number not seen before. Over the past 10 months, the outlet identified more cases of “belt-tightening” in the social sphere than it did during all of 2025. The outlet did not provide exact figures.

Regions forced to cut social spending include not only “poor” regions such as Karelia and the Vladimir region, but also industrial, resource-extracting regions such as the Kemerovo and Sverdlovsk regions, Krasnoyarsk Krai, and Yakutia.

Sharp cuts to social spending began in 2025. The study’s authors link the cuts to the end of the wartime economic boom of 2023–2024.

items.title: Kremlin plans to rank Russia’s ‘traditional values,’ placing patriotism above life and mercy
items.summary:
The Kremlin is drafting legislation that will establish a hierarchy of “traditional values,” said Alexander Kharichev, head of the Russian Presidential Administration’s department for monitoring and analyzing social processes.

Kharichev said the hierarchy will appear in a bill on patriotic upbringing and civic education. He made the remarks at a session titled “Values of the Future: From Definition to Actualization” during the “Creating the Future” symposium.

“Sovereignty values are recognized as the core — patriotism, the continuity of generations, and, in fact, responsibility for the fate of one’s homeland, and so on,” he said, according to the Russian state news agency TASS.

“That bloc of values relating to patriotism is recognized as fundamental in this hierarchy of values,” Kharichev stressed.

Kharichev said the bill is “almost ready” and will be submitted to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, soon.

The list of “traditional values” is set out in a presidential decree from November 2022. The document lists “traditional values” in the following order:

Life, dignity, human rights and freedoms, patriotism, civic consciousness, service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate, high moral ideals, a strong family, creative labor, the priority of the spiritual over the material, humanism, mercy, justice, collectivism, mutual assistance and mutual respect, historical memory and the continuity of generations, the unity of the peoples of Russia.

items.title: Russian government approves bill regulating self-driving cars, taxis, and trams, Kommersant reports
items.summary:
The Russian government approved the final version of a bill called “On Highly Automated Vehicles” on November 12, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported after reviewing the document.

The bill took more than five years to draft. Russia’s Transport Ministry has worked on it since 2021, and the document lays out general requirements and operating rules for self-driving cars, trucks, taxis, and trams.

The bill will also, among other things, regulate liability in traffic accidents, set requirements for protecting self-driving vehicles’ software, and specify the systems autonomous vehicles must carry.

The bill has not yet been submitted to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, but will be “in the near future,” Kommersant reported.

A range of self-driving vehicles, including taxis, trams, and trucks, have operated in Russia since 2018, usually with an operator in the cabin as backup.

Moscow already operates Russia’s first self-driving tram, which has run on route No. 10 from Kulakov Street to the Shchukinskaya metro station since September 2025. In November 2026, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin promised that the number of self-driving trams would rise to 15 by the end of 2026 and to 25 by 2027.

items.title: ‘You could even have a TV show about it’: Europe struggles to choose its representative for Ukraine peace talks
items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin. November 3, 2026 
 The United States, Russia, and Ukraine will expand the format of their trilateral peace talks to include Europe, U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff said yesterday evening, after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Witkoff said European representatives would join the next meeting. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he said. 

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov indicated at a briefing today that Moscow does not object to European participation, though his comments stopped short of confirming that Russia has given its final consent. Peskov said “a real decision on dialogue in an expanded format” could come once the Kremlin “understands their real intentions and readiness to contribute to the peace process.”

“If the Europeans have someone who is at least somehow authorized to negotiate, if the Europeans genuinely have the desire, then of course we will be ready to talk with them,” Peskov said. He also said bilateral contacts with the Europeans are not yet under discussion, though Russia is ready for that as well.

Still, it remains unclear who will represent Europe in the talks. The question dominated a summit of EU heads of state taking place in Dublin yesterday and today, even though the gathering had not originally been planned to address the Russia–Ukraine war.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, addressing deep divisions in Europe over the candidacy, said: “You could even have a TV show about it.” As Politico reports…

items.title: Russian strikes kill three in Ukraine, injure several others, including children
items.summary:
Russian forces attacked several regions of Ukraine overnight on November 13, striking Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Rivne, and the Kharkiv region.

In Zaporizhzhia, a Russian strike killed a 17-year-old and wounded 13 people, including five children. In Odesa, a Russian strike killed two people and injured seven, destroying a one-story residential building and sparking a fire. Elsewhere in the city, the strike damaged 11 cars.

In the Kharkiv region, a strike on residential buildings injured seven people, including two children. A married couple was rescued from the rubble of a destroyed building.

In Rivne, Russian shelling damaged a residential building, wounding six people, including two children. The shelling forced the evacuation of 42 residents.

In Kyiv’s Shevchenkivskyi district, a strike hit a hospital, sparking a fire and partially collapsing the building’s second floor. One person was injured, and 37 people were evacuated.

items.title: Ukrainian drone attacks have turned Russian airports into a nightmare of endless delays, overcrowded terminals, and no information. One traveler recounts a night of chaos.
items.summary:
Russian airports have been paralyzed by Ukrainian drone attacks. Russian regions impose “carpet protocols,” suspending all flights, almost every day. This leads to flight cancellations and delays — as a rule, neither passengers nor airport staff can predict how long they will last. People caught in this situation before a flight are left alone with their problems: their plans are disrupted, staff give no clear instructions, and airlines try to save money on compensation. At the same time, the airports themselves were not designed to handle passengers from dozens of flights getting stranded simultaneously.

In this piece, a Meduza reader describes what she had to deal with at Sheremetyevo, where a carpet protocol was imposed for an entire night in early November. We illustrated her account with photographs from four Moscow airports, taken on days when a carpet protocol was imposed in the region.

I had already checked in at Sheremetyevo and was walking toward the gate when a text message arrived: my flight had been pushed back from 1 a.m. to 6:30 a.m. The delay appeared on the departure board at the same moment.

A crowd of passengers walked past me, having just been brought back from the airfield. Their plane had already begun taxiing toward the runway when it stopped. After two hours of waiting on the tarmac, the passengers were returned to the airport without explanation, as if everyone already understood why.

No one explained what I should do next or whether I was entitled to any compensation for the delay. A Google search told me passengers are owed water after a…
items.t: Ukrainian drone attacks have turned Russian airports into a nightmare of endless delays, overcrowded terminals, and no information. One traveler recounts a night of chaos.

Details of the system appear in the passport of Roskomnadzor’s digital transformation program for 2026 and the 2027–2028 planning period.

The document says the system runs on a Russian-made model deployed on in-house infrastructure, and no further details have been disclosed.

Roskomnadzor has integrated the AI-based technology into the Automated System for Ensuring the Security of the Russian Segment of the Internet, where it supplements TSPU, Russia’s existing internet traffic filtering system.

Forbes Russia had reported in early 2026 that Roskomnadzor planned to create and roll out an AI-based traffic filtering mechanism, and at the time, the agency was expected to use Astra AI, developed by Astra Group.

Amid internet blocking and the crackdown on VPN use, Russia’s federal budget for the next three years earmarks a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering.

In April 2024, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported that Roskomnadzor planned to use AI-based systems to maintain its registry of banned information. In October 2026, the Digital Development Ministry proposed using AI to detect and block VPNs. Experts warned at the time that using such models, especially in the early stages, could lead to erroneous blockings.

Mash specified that the vehicle was a Toyota Fortuner SUV belonging to Sergei Zavorotny. The Telegram channel described him as an “international affairs journalist” who had “held government positions in Ukraine.”

The explosive device was attached to the underside of the car on the driver’s side and detonated as the vehicle was being driven down the street, Telegram channels reported . Zavorotny was behind the wheel, according to Shot and Mash. He survived the explosion but is in serious condition, Telegram channels said.

The Investigative Committee, a Russian federal investigating authority, said a criminal case had been opened over the car explosion on Kirovogradskaya Street in Moscow. The statement did not name the driver, and it was unclear what charge was being pursued.

Sergei Zavorotny worked at the pro-Kremlin Russian tabloid Komsomolskaya Pravda, and from 2003 to 2004 headed the press service for the Rodina party’s faction in Russia’s State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament. He later became the press secretary for Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, who held the post from 2010 to 2014 under Viktor Yanukovych.

items.title: Cost of insuring Russian data centers against drone attacks skyrockets — rising more than 100-fold in some cases
items.summary:
Insurance for data centers in Russia has risen sharply, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported.

In the first half of 2026, insurance cost 0.03–0.06% of the value of insured property. Ukrainian attacks on data centers belonging to Yandex and Sberbank began in October, and rates have since risen to 1–5%. In some cases, the price increase amounts to more than 100-fold.

The Russian National Reinsurance Company, which is owned by Russia’s central bank, also tightened conditions for insuring data centers in October, setting a base rate of 1% for insured amounts of 10 billion rubles.

The company also compiled a list of locations where it reinsures facilities on a case-by-case basis, under individually negotiated terms.

As a result, companies are reducing insurance coverage or excluding certain risks from their policies, experts say.

Ukrainian drones first attacked data centers belonging to three Russian companies — Yandex, Sberbank, and VK — in October. Russian troops had earlier attacked data centers in Ukraine.

Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s Volgograd region, sparking a fire at an industrial facility and causing fatalities, regional governor Andrey Bocharov said.

Bocharov said overnight on November 13 that the fall of  “drone debris” at a plant in Volgograd’s southern industrial zone had caused “localized fires.” By morning, he added that four plant employees had died and two were hospitalized.

Ukrainian monitoring channels reported that the Volgograd oil refinery, owned by Lukoil, was on fire.

According to the Telegram channel Exilenova+, this was the 13th attack on the Volgograd refinery since the start of the full-scale war. In early October, Reuters reported that the refinery had completely halted oil processing after another Ukrainian drone attack.

Lines began forming at gas stations in Volgograd after the drone attack, local outlets reported . V1.ru said popular gasoline brands at chain gas stations rose by 50 kopecks overnight on November 13.

Ukrainian drones also headed toward Moscow overnight on November 13. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 467 drones flew toward the Moscow region from the evening of November 12 until morning. He said air defense forces destroyed most of the drones “at distant frontiers” and neutralized 144 more as they approached Moscow.

Restrictions on arrivals and departures were imposed overnight at all four Moscow airports (Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky) and lifted by morning.

items.title: Russia is using seized foreign companies to funnel billions of rubles into its war effort, Bloomberg reports
items.summary:
Russian authorities have placed Russian subsidiaries of foreign companies under temporary administration, and those companies are transferring billions of rubles to meet military needs, Bloomberg reported.

For the most part, after a change in management, these companies have sent funds to Putin’s People’s Front, which uses the money to buy drones, vehicles, communications systems, and other equipment for Russian troops.

Paint manufacturer AkzoNobel has sent about two billion rubles for military needs, according to company statements and Russian media reports. Brewing company AB InBev Efes, retailer Metro , and electrical equipment manufacturer DKC each transferred one billion rubles.

The Bell reported in October that Poland’s Can-Pack, whose Russian assets were placed under temporary administration, transferred 1.5 billion rubles to the fund earlier this year in two installments. The former Russian unit of Denmark’s Rockwool transferred 600 million rubles.

These payments are modest compared with state spending on the war, which is expected to exceed 17 trillion rubles this year, but they give company management a way to show their support for the authorities, Bloomberg said.

The Dutch company AkzoNobel said its parent completely lost control of its Russian assets and learns about them only through media reports. Belgian-Turkish AB InBev Efes and Italian DKC Europe Srl did not comment.

In recent months, Russian authorities have stepped up placing foreign companies’ assets under temporary administration. Assets transferred to temporary administration include those of…

items.title: Sadiq Khan joins Labour figures urging PM not to water down electric vehicle targets – as it happened
items.summary:
This blog is now closed

On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it.

She said:

I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work.

The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second.

Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said:

The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch.

He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes.

It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’

I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not…

items.title: Trump won't save Ukraine. But Marine Le Pen's betrayal could be worse | Mujtaba Rahman
items.summary:
European leaders need urgently to prepare for a far-right French president who would cut off Kyiv’s financial lifeline

Europe is consumed by two debates that matter less than it thinks, while neglecting one that matters enormously. The first is who should represent the EU in negotiations with Russia. This is largely irrelevant because there is little prospect of serious Ukraine peace talks before the end of winter - despite the fanfare that has surrounded discussions in Abu Dhabi this week. Russia has powerful incentives to escalate the war over the coming months in an attempt to break Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale.

The second is Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine. This matters less than it once did – and not only because he is now more constrained by a Democratic Congress. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has provided no new US military aid to Kyiv. American weapons sales remain important to Ukraine’s war effort, but Trump’s military interventions in the Middle East have further strained supplies of the weapons Ukraine needs most – notably Patriot interceptors.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

items.title: Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul Taylor
items.summary:
A deal giving Moscow a slice of Ukrainian territory and sanctions relief could be on the table in weeks – yet European leaders are busy squabbling

Donald Trump has lost substantial power over domestic policy after last week’s devastating midterm losses, but his ability to cement his legacy by upending US foreign policy remains largely intact.

There is every reason to fear a ”great betrayal” of Ukraine in the coming weeks, one that would reward Vladimir Putin for Russia’s war of aggression against Kyiv, and also do lasting damage to the European security order. Yet lilliputian European leaders are too busy squabbling over who should represent them in future peace talks to focus on how to prevent a sellout. Despite fundamental European interests being at stake in this week’s three-way US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations in Abu Dhabi, Europe is relegated to a side room, represented by a posse of officials from the UK, France, Germany, the EU and Nato.
